[strategy/white-papers/security/security-standards-enablement-brief.md#1-purpose-and-scope]

## 1. Purpose and Scope

This brief provides a proposal package for the security standards authoring group.

The objective is to accelerate standards development by supplying:

- A prioritized candidate list of the top 20 security standards to consider
- A curated list of supporting architecture and strategy documents
- A sequencing model for intake and authoring
- Clear handoff expectations between architecture and standards functions

This brief does not prescribe how the standards team should write standards. It supplies context, priorities, dependencies, and source references.

---
page_texts.4:
[strategy/white-papers/security/security-standards-enablement-brief.md#2-why-this-deliverable-form]

## 2. Why This Deliverable Form

A short enablement brief is recommended over a long white paper for this use case because it is:

- Faster for standards authors to consume and triage
- Easier to convert into standards backlog items
- Easier to maintain as guidance evolves
- Better for governance reviews that need decisions and dependencies at a glance

For committee presentation, this brief can be paired with a 5-7 slide intake deck.

---
page_texts.5:
[strategy/white-papers/security/security-standards-enablement-brief.md#3-decision-request-to-standards-group]

## 3. Decision Request to Standards Group

The standards authoring group is asked to:

1. Approve the proposed Top 20 standards candidate list as intake scope
2. Confirm the Wave 1, Wave 2, and Wave 3 sequencing model
3. Confirm use of the supporting-document index in this brief as input references
4. Assign standards ownership and target publication windows

---
page_texts.6:
[strategy/white-papers/security/security-standards-enablement-brief.md#4-selection-logic-used-for-top-20]

## 4. Selection Logic Used for Top 20

The candidate list is prioritized using four filters:

1. Regulatory and contractual impact (HIPAA, HITRUST, NIST, SOC 2, FedRAMP-aligned controls)
2. Zero Trust architecture dependency (identity, segmentation, verification, monitoring)
3. Risk reduction value (blast-radius reduction, breach likelihood reduction, response capability)
4. Cross-domain enablement (documents and controls reused by multiple standards)

---
page_texts.7:
[strategy/white-papers/security/security-standards-enablement-brief.md#5-proposed-top-20-standards-candidate-set]

## 5. Proposed Top 20 Standards Candidate Set

| Priority | Candidate Standard | Primary Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Enterprise IAM Framework | Unified identity controls, lifecycle governance |
| 2 | MFA Enforcement | Phishing-resistant authentication baseline |
| 3 | Privileged Access Management (PAM/JIT) | Least privilege for elevated access |
| 4 | Encryption and Key Management | Consistent at-rest and in-transit data protection |
| 5 | Network Segmentation and Micro-segmentation | Lateral movement containment |
| 6 | Secure SDLC and DevSecOps Gates | Build-time and deploy-time security assurance |
| 7 | API Security and Integration Controls | Consistent protection of service interfaces |
| 8 | Data Classification and Handling | Tiered protection by data sensitivity |
| 9 | Data Loss Prevention (DLP) | Exfiltration prevention and policy enforcement |
| 10 | Container and Kubernetes Security | Workload and orchestration hardening |
| 11 | Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) | Continuous endpoint threat visibility |
| 12 | Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) | Misconfiguration and drift control |
| 13 | Vulnerability Management and Remediation SLAs | Prioritized remediation lifecycle |
| 14 | Patch and Configuration Baselines | Time-bound hardening and patch compliance |
| 15 | Centralized Logging and Audit | Forensics and compliance evidence quality |
| 16 | SIEM and Detection Engineering | Correlated detection and alert fidelity |
| 17 | Incident Response and Breach Procedures | Repeatable containment and recovery execution |
| 18 | Break Glass Emergency Access | Controlled emergency access with accountability |
| 19 | Third-Party and Supply Chain Security | Vendor and dependency risk governance |
| 20 | Compliance Monitoring and Evidence Automation | Continuous audit readiness and control attestations |

---

[strategy/white-papers/security/security-standards-enablement-brief.md#wave-1-foundation]

### Wave 1 (Foundation)

Candidate standards: 1, 2, 4, 5, 15

Rationale:

- Establishes identity, crypto, segmentation, and audit baseline
- Creates immediate risk reduction and audit value
- Unlocks downstream standards with shared controls
page_texts.19:
[strategy/white-papers/security/security-standards-enablement-brief.md#wave-2-application-and-data]

### Wave 2 (Application and Data)

Candidate standards: 6, 7, 8, 10, 16, 17

Rationale:

- Moves security left into delivery pipelines and APIs
- Hardens data and workload planes
- Improves detection and response readiness
page_texts.20:
[strategy/white-papers/security/security-standards-enablement-brief.md#wave-3-operational-hardening-and-governance]

### Wave 3 (Operational Hardening and Governance)

Candidate standards: 3, 9, 11, 12, 13, 14, 18, 19, 20

Rationale:

- Completes runtime hardening and governance maturity
- Strengthens emergency operations and third-party assurance
- Institutionalizes continuous compliance evidence production

### Architecture Team Responsibilities

- Provide guidance context, ABB/RAD references, and strategic rationale
- Maintain supporting-document index and dependency map
- Advise on architecture implications and control interactions
page_texts.23:
[strategy/white-papers/security/security-standards-enablement-brief.md#standards-authoring-team-responsibilities]

### Standards Authoring Team Responsibilities

- Author enforceable standards language and control requirements
- Define conformance targets, exceptions, and enforcement mechanics
- Own publication, revision cycle, and standards lifecycle governance

---
page_texts.25:
[strategy/white-papers/security/security-standards-enablement-brief.md#assumptions]

### Assumptions

- Standards authorship process and quality controls are already established
- Standards group can fetch referenced documents directly from repository paths
- Security governance forums are available for wave-based prioritization decisions
page_texts.26:
[strategy/white-papers/security/security-standards-enablement-brief.md#risks]

### Risks

- Overlap with existing standards if intake boundaries are not clarified early
- Dependency bottlenecks if key supporting documents are delayed
- Inconsistent control language across waves if template discipline is weak
page_texts.27:
[strategy/white-papers/security/security-standards-enablement-brief.md#mitigations]

### Mitigations

- Run an intake normalization pass before authoring begins
- Confirm wave-level dependency readiness at the start of each wave
- Use a common standards template and reviewer checklist across all waves

---

- Approve candidate list and wave sequencing
- Assign authors and review leads for Wave 1
- Confirm which backlog support documents are needed immediately
page_texts.30:

### Days 31-60

- Draft and review Wave 1 standards
- Build compliance mapping pack for Wave 1
- Prepare Wave 2 intake package
page_texts.31:
[strategy/white-papers/security/security-standards-enablement-brief.md#days-61-90]

### Days 61-90

- Publish Wave 1 standards
- Initiate Wave 2 drafting
- Baseline KPI tracking for adoption, exceptions, and control evidence quality
